items.title: Texas Housing Insight | November 2026 | Texas Real Estate Research Center
items.description: Texas Housing Insight | November 2026 Texas’ housing market continued to soften in September as rising mortgage rates, inflation, and affordability challenges restrained buyer demand, slowed sales, and kept home-price growth muted. By Yanling Mayer quick links September continued to see a pullback in market momentum, as seasonal cooling combined with rising mortgage rates, rising inflationary pressures, and affordability constraints dampened buyer activity. Existing-home sales declined from a year earlier, and market activity remained subdued. Fewer than two out of every ten homes listed for sale during the month were sold (1.5 homes), highlighting slower inventory turnover and longer marketing times amid challenging demand conditions. Year to date, sales remain modestly ahead of last year’s pace, suggesting housing demand has not deteriorated from last year. Home-price growth remained muted. Statewide home prices were essentially unchanged from a year ago, as gains in a handful of markets were offset by continued weakness elsewhere. Major metropolitan areas, including Austin, Dallas, and San Antonio, continued to experience measurable downward price pressure, while Houston and the Fort Worth metro division showed signs of modest stabilization. On the supply side, inventory levels eased seasonally following their summer peak, consistent with typical market patterns heading into the fall and winter. Nevertheless, overall inventory remains only slightly below peak summer levels, indicating that the inventory condition remains favorable to buyers. Looking ahead, the housing market is expected to remain soft through the remainder of the year. Mortgage rates are near current multi-decade highs, limiting purchasing power and sidelining prospective buyers. Unless financing conditions improve meaningfully, housing demand is likely to remain restrained, resulting in slower sales and weak prices. Disclaimer: The September 2026 figures are based on more complete data and have been revised from their initial release. Year-Over-Year Sales Down Table 1: September 2026 State & National Sales Notes: The sales numbers reflect actual sales, not the seasonally adjusted rate. Source: Texas REALTORS® and National Association of REALTORS® and U.S. Census Bureau data In September, Texas recorded 20,200 existing-home sales statewide, down 1.6 percent year over year (YoY). September marked a second consecutive month of YoY sales declines. As of 3Q2026, year-to-date (YTD) sales volume rose 3.3 percent from last year. As of September, median existing-home price was $325,000, softening slightly from August’s $330,000 and unchanged from a year ago. Nationally, seasonally unadjusted existing home sales were down 3.9 percent YoY, a second consecutive month of sales declines, while YTD sales volumes remained slightly ahead of last year’s pace. National median price reached $422,700, maintaining a steady growth pace at about 1.4 percent YoY. September’s new-home sales in U.S. declined 3.4 percent YoY. As of the third quarter, YTD new-home sales were 2.9 percent below last year’s pace. Monthly Market Snapshot: September Sales and Inventory Trends Table 2: Texas Housing Market Indicators Notes: The turnover rate is calculated as pending sales divided by inventory, where inventory is the average of month-beginning and month-ending inventory Source: Texas Real Estate Research Center analysis of Data Relevance Project and Texas REALTORS® data Homes sold in September spent an average of 65 days on the market (DoM), compared to a similar 63 days a year ago. Inventory turnover was slow at 15 percent, down from 16.2 percent a year ago. At this pace, fewer than two in ten existing homes (1.5 homes) on the market went under contract during the month. The median seller price cut remained similar to a year ago at $15,000, equivalent to roughly 4.5 percent of the initial listing price. As of September, active inventory is at a 5.7-month supply, similar to a year ago. The unsold inventory has an average DoM of 98 days, compared to a DoM of 65 days among the sold. New Listing Activity Eases Seasonally, Remaining Near Year-Ago Levels Figure 1: Monthly New-Listing Activity, 2026 Source : Texas Real Estate Research Center analysis of Data Relevance Project, Texas REALTORS® data Statewide, 47,580 new listings were recorded, down 2.1 percent from August, reflecting the typical seasonal slowdown as the market moves into the fall and winter months. September’s new listings remained 2.1 percent above September 2025 levels. Through September, year-to-date listing activity was largely unchanged from last year, edging down just 0.3 percent. Among the major metros, YoY new-listing activity increased 7.7 percent in Austin, 3 percent in Houston, and 3.8 percent in San Antonio, while DFW posted a 2.0 decline, continuing a stretch of relatively weak new-listing activity that began in April (see Table 4). The YTD activity in Austin, Houston, and San Antonio all remained slightly ahead of last year’s pace; in DFW it trailed by 3.2 percent. Inventory Levels Slightly Below the Summer Peak Figure 2: Monthly Active Inventory, 2026 Source : Texas Real Estate Research Center analysis of Data Relevance Project, Texas REALTORS® data At the end of September, the for-sale inventory stood at nearly 154,200 listings, up 5.6 percent from a year earlier. Although inventory continued its seasonal easing, September levels remained only slightly below the peak reached in July. Inventory trends varied across the major metropolitan areas (see Table 4). YoY inventory increased 3.9 percent in Austin, 7.3 percent in Houston, and 1.6 percent in San Antonio, while DFW recorded a 6 percent decline. Houston remained the only major metro where inventory levels have largely held near their summer peak since July. Other markets experienced more noticeable seasonal declines. items.title: Multifamily Rebalancing Advances
items.description: Multifamily Rebalancing Advances Nov 17, 2026 | 4 min read U.S. Multifamily Capital Markets | Q3 2026 Multifamily fundamentals continued to rebalance as occupancy edged higher, rent recovery broadened, and the construction pipeline contracted, creating a firmer foundation heading into 2027. Download the full report Experts David Amsterdam President, Capital Markets | U.S. David Goodhue Executive Managing Director | Boston & Head of Multifamily Capital Markets | U.S Rachael Rothman Director, National Capital Markets Research View All [5] Experts Share Article Top Highlights Occupancy continued to improve, edging higher to 95.7% despite more subdued leasing activity in the third quarter. Demand moderated from the exceptional second-quarter pace, with absorption trailing new deliveries but remaining well above year-ago levels. The development pipeline continued to contract, improving the longer-term supply outlook while near-term pressure remains concentrated in select markets. Rent recovery broadened across markets, with 40 of the Top 60 markets posting positive annual rent growth. Capital markets remain selective, as underlying transaction activity and pricing continue to reflect price discovery rather than a broad recovery in liquidity. Key Statistics Multifamily fundamentals remain resilient as the market continues to work through recent supply additions and the development pipeline moderates. Occupancy Remains Resilient National occupancy remained healthy in Q3 2026 as markets continued to absorb recently delivered units. While conditions vary across geographies, supply-constrained markets continue to demonstrate particularly strong operating fundamentals, while higher-supply markets remain more competitive. Source: Colliers Research, RealPage, MSCI Real Capital Analytics Rent Recovery Broadens Rent performance improved across a broader share of markets during the third quarter, signaling a more widespread recovery in pricing conditions. Performance remains uneven, however, with supply levels and local demand continuing to drive meaningful differences between markets. Supply Risk Remains Concentrated The national development pipeline continued to contract during the third quarter as financing challenges, elevated construction costs, and capital constraints limited new development. While the pullback should ease supply pressure nationally over time, several markets still face elevated construction pipelines that will continue to influence near-term performance. Capital Markets Navigate a Selective Recovery Investment activity continues to reflect a market in transition. Multifamily transaction volume reached $114.1 billion in Q3 2026, but the increase primarily reflected an entity-level merger rather than a broad recovery in liquidity. Excluding entity-level transactions, volume declined 7% to $44.5 billion, while apartment pricing remained under pressure. Investors continue to prioritize durable cash flow, realistic acquisition pricing, and manageable refinancing exposure as the market works through continued price discovery. Source: Colliers Research, MSCI Real Capital Analytics Sector Spotlight: Seniors Housing Seniors housing is benefiting from a combination of powerful demographic demand, improving operating performance, and constrained new supply. Growth in the older U.S. population is expanding the long-term demand base for independent living, assisted living, and nursing care, while limited development is supporting occupancy and rent fundamentals. Capital markets activity is also strengthening as investors respond to improving fundamentals and the sector's long-term demographic outlook. The report examines operating trends, regional performance, transaction activity, and the investment landscape across seniors housing and care. Looking Ahead Multifamily enters the final months of 2026 with healthy occupancy, a shrinking development pipeline, and a broader rent recovery, creating a more constructive operating backdrop. At the same time, capital markets remain selective, and refinancing pressure continues to create challenges and opportunities across the sector. Heading into 2027, the pace of new supply, local demand trends, and financing conditions will remain critical to determining where operating performance and investment opportunities strengthen most. U.S. Market Overviews The report features key statistics across the Top 60 U.S. multifamily markets, along with detailed spotlights on 15 select markets: Baltimore, Cincinnati, Denver, Greensboro, Indianapolis, Las Vegas, Memphis, Nassau County, Northern/Central New Jersey, Orange County, Pittsburgh, Richmond, San Diego, St. Louis, and Washington, D.C. Explore local trends in occupancy, rent growth, demand, supply, development activity, and investment performance across each market. items.title: BTR Operators Push For Treasury To Loosen Rules As Consolidation Looms – BisNow
items.description: The build-to-rent sector is facing a second round of wrangling with the government after a hard-fought battle with lawmakers over the summer to keep the industry from facing steep regulations as part of the housing bill that made its way through Congress . BTR operators and industry advocates are pushing for changes to proposed rules from the Department of the Treasury that will dictate how the restrictions on BTR operators from the 21st Century Road to Housing Act are implemented. Operators in the sector say the rules could hamper new development and, regardless of what’s adjusted, expect consolidation to sweep across the sector. “Hopefully that gets adjusted, because that will have a severe impact on capital flows and ultimately the building of new homes and new rental communities,” Richard Ross , CEO of Atlanta-based Quinn Residences , said of the proposed rules. Unsplash/Michael Tuszynski The proposed regulations require large institutional investors, which are defined in the original legislation as firms with at least 350 single-family rental units, to adopt written BTR programs before they purchase a community and would preclude BTR operators from purchasing properties more than 18 months after the home received its certificate of occupancy. Ross, whose firm has developed or purchased 5,200 homes across 34 communities since its founding in 2020, wrote in a letter submitted as a public comment to Treasury that it can frequently take two years or more to stabilize a newly built community. The two new rules would make it more difficult for homebuilders to sell excess inventory to build-to-rent operators, hampering activity in a pool of properties that BTR operators have long dipped into, Ross told Bisnow . His letter was one of more than 100 public comments filed so far. Other operators and industry groups, including the nonpartisan trade association National Rental Home Council , are still crafting their own submissions, CEO Adrianne Todman said. The public comment period closes on Nov. 23. “The Treasury Department has put forward some thoughtful rules where they're trying to thread the needle very carefully by making sure they are properly implementing the legislative ban on investors being able to buy homes but also making sure that it's not having any detrimental impacts to the housing marketplace and particularly the rental marketplace,” Todman said. The push to shift the rules follows the first bout of uncertainty that shrouded the BTR sector when the Road to Housing legislation was originally being debated. The bill debuted with strict restrictions on the BTR business model that threatened to upend the sector. It took intense lobbying for the rules to shift. Investment in the sector was severely scaled back during that debate, as investors waited to see what the final legislation would include. “When there was a threat to being able to build new rental supply via build-to-rent, we saw that there was millions of dollars and thousands of units that went on the sidelines and that those resources were frozen,” Todman said. “Those resources are thawing out a bit, and we want to make sure that they thaw out even more.” The push for clear guidelines gained new momentum after Democrats won control of both houses of Congress in the midterm elections. Some senators-elect ran on campaigns explicitly against corporate ownership of homes, including James Talarico in Texas and Josh Turek in Iowa. Talarico’s website includes a call to “ban Wall Street from buying up housing stock to enrich wealthy investors while making it harder for families to afford homes,” and Turek’s platform includes a call to ban private equity firms from purchasing single-family homes. The Road to Housing legislation adds new compliance standards and an element of federal oversight, including public reporting requirements for large operators, that are expected to lead to a wave of buyouts and mergers across the sector. The consolidation is likely coming regardless of where Treasury lands on its rules, as smaller players are squeezed by costs that large operators that benefit from economies of scale can more easily absorb. “You put it all together, it's just a tougher backdrop for them to really justify their existence,” said Haendel St. Juste , equity research analyst at Mizuho , who upgraded the two major publicly traded single-family rental firms to outperform in September. Unsplash/Nate Johnston New compliance costs for operators with at least 350 units but not thousands will raise operating costs for smaller BTR firms around the same time that the private equity funds backing those platforms reach the end of their lives. A substantial amount of the debt backing private BTR and SFR firms was issued around five to seven years ago and is reaching the end of its natural life cycle, leaving operators facing significantly higher debt service costs to stay in business, St. Juste said. Nontraded SFR REIT VineBrook Homes Trust suspended share buybacks earlier this month after ending a tender offer that drew three times as many shares as the REIT sought to buy. VineBrook, which has 20,500 units in 21 states, flagged an upcoming $650.8M debt maturity within a year as a driving factor behind the shift in strategy. For Invitation Homes and American Homes 4 Rent , the two biggest publicly traded single-family rental firms, the legislation creates a unique and sizable rollup opportunity, St. Juste wrote in a September analysis. The two REITs have trailed the broader REIT index by about 13 percentage points this year, according to Mizuho’s September report, and investors see upside potential in the wide gap that exists between the firms’ public valuations and the value of the properties in their portfolios. The REITs have been using that gap to sell homes and buy back stock at an attractive valuation, a trend that is expected to continue into 2027. items.title: Zillow: CPI Shelter Forecast, November 2026
items.description: Zillow: CPI Shelter Forecast, November 2026 Zillow forecasts 3.0% rent inflation, 3.6% OER inflation annually in October, as measured by the Consumer Price Index. Written by Treh Manhertz on November 17, 2026 New shelter inflation numbers from the Bureau of Labor Statistics are scheduled to be released on Thursday, December 10, 2026 at 8:30 ET. Key Takeaway CPI housing inflation is expected to firm into the end of the year. We currently forecast annual rent inflation to finish 2026 around 3.0% and OER near 3.5%. Part of the year-end rise is mechanical, as the BLS folded October 2025's increase ,missed during the government shutdown, into April 2026. This adjustment will add about 0.3 points to the true underlying annual rate until April 2027. From last month's forecast, the year-end outlook was revised up for OER (3.44% to 3.53%) and down for rent (3.06% to 3.04%). New-lease rents have been growing at their fastest pace of 2025-2026, no longer pulling down housing inflation measures. Forecasts for on-market rents have been revised higher for the past few months. items.title: Pretium Expands Real Estate Debt Platform
items.description: Pretium Expands Real Estate Debt Platform November 19, 2026 --> Addition of Hilltop Capital Partners Enables the Firm to Deploy Capital to the U.K. Housing Market NEW YORK, November 19, 2026 – Pretium, a specialized investment firm with approximately $70 billion in assets under management, today announced it is expanding its residential real estate debt platform, further enabling the flow of capital to real estate investors, developers, and homebuilders. Since launching its residential debt platform in December 2024, Pretium has lent approximately $8 billion for the purpose of new housing construction and the renovation of existing homes. Building on its existing model, Pretium is adding the team from Hilltop Capital Partners (“Hilltop”), a specialized U.K.-based institutional capital advisor, investment manager and principal lender, to its vertically integrated residential real estate platform. Led by Paul Oberschneider and Tiger Craft, Hilltop has grown into a leading platform for residential development finance across the U.K since its founding in 2019. “The U.K. faces a housing shortage of approximately four to five million homes, and the Hilltop team has built an impressive platform supporting homebuilders, developers and sponsors with flexible, solutions-oriented capital,” said Jonathan Pruzan, Co-President at Pretium. “This expansion is a natural extension of the model we’ve built in the U.S., and we are pleased to welcome the Hilltop team to Pretium. Our real estate debt platform provides much-needed capital to grow the housing stock, while delivering value to our investors.” “U.K. homebuilders need capital that understands development risk and the full ecosystem of finance. Joining the Pretium ecosystem provides us the scale the U.K. homebuilder market requires right now, and I’m excited about what this means for the business in the years ahead,” said Paul Oberschneider, Chairman of Hilltop. "We are thrilled to be joining Pretium. The firm's depth of talent and focus on residential markets make this a natural fit for Hilltop. This gives us the infrastructure and backing to deliver flexible financing to U.K. residential developers and sponsors with greater speed, scale and certainty of execution," said Tiger Craft, CEO of Hilltop. About Pretium Pretium is a specialized investment firm focused on U.S. residential real estate equity and credit. Pretium was founded in 2012 and has built an integrated analytical and operational ecosystem within the U.S. housing and credit markets and believes that its insight and experience within these markets create a strategic advantage. Pretium’s platform has approximately $70 billion in assets and employs 7,000 people across 45+ offices as of June 30, 2026, including its New York headquarters, Miami, London, Abu Dhabi, Bangalore, Seoul and Sydney. Please visit www.pretium.com for additional information. About Hilltop Founded in 2019, Hilltop Credit Partners Limited, trading as Hilltop Capital Partners, is a London-based real estate credit investment adviser and principal lender, focused on providing capital solutions to residential property developers across the UK and Europe. Funds advised by Hilltop have provided c. $300 million in debt funding to support the construction of over 1,000 residential units across the UK. ### Media Contact Brenna Karp Pretium [email protected]

items.title: New Home Market Update
items.description: New Home Market Update Zonda tracks 85% of the production new home market across the United States. Given the proprietary database, Zonda is uniquely positioned to capture trends and changes in the new home market. This report showcases the latest housing trends in the new home market for October 2026. November 20, 2026 – 5 min read Table of Content: The new home market has slipped into underperformance October marked another step backward for the new home market. Sales declined 3.1% month-over-month and 11.7% year-over-year, a considerably steeper annual decline than September's 4.6% drop. The weakness was widespread, with pending sales declining year-over-year across all of Zonda's select markets. The national Zonda Market Ranking also slipped into slightly underperforming territory for the first time since December 2022. The latest figures reinforce what builders have been telling us for months. Zonda's October builder sentiment survey found that 86% of builders reported slower-than-expected demand, up from 84% in September. In their comments, builders pointed to declining traffic, limited buyer urgency, and growing frustration with the effectiveness of incentives. “One of the biggest challenges for builders right now is generating enough buyer interest in the first place,” said Sarah Bonnarens, director of economic research for Zonda and NewHomeSource. “Builders still have an advantage when it comes to pricing and financing flexibility, but those tools can only do so much when buyer traffic is down. The challenge is keeping sales moving without putting even more pressure on margins.” The annual decline in new home sales deepened Zonda's new home sales metric counts the number of new home contract sales each month and accounts for both cancellations and seasonality. This metric shows there were 638,568 new homes sold in October on a seasonally adjusted annualized rate. This was a decline of 3.1% from last month and a drop of 11.7% from a year ago. On a non-seasonally adjusted basis, 50,770 homes were sold, 11.6% lower than last year and 2.8% below the same month in 2019. Incentives remain a key feature of the new home market, helping to sustain sales activity amid ongoing affordability pressures. In October, 64% of new home communities offered incentives on to-be-built homes and 83% on quick move-in supply. Note, these are only publicly available incentives so they will underrepresent overall usage. All select markets saw PSI fall YOY Zonda's New Home Pending Sales Index (PSI) was created to help account for fluctuations in supply by combining both total sales volume with the average sales rate per month per community. The October PSI came in at 122.8, representing an 11.4% decline from the same month last year. The index is currently 29.5% below cycle highs. On a month-over-month basis, seasonally adjusted new home sales decreased 1.9%. The markets that held up the best relative to last year were Minneapolis (-0.3%), Charlotte (-1.1%), and Tampa (-3.5%). Minneapolis was down compared to the last year but grew 10.2% month-over-month. Inversely, the metros that performed the worst year-over-year were Los Angeles/OC (-31.4%), Riverside/San Bernardino (-28.4%), and Denver (-26.3%). On a monthly basis, Minneapolis, Sacramento, and Denver were the best performing markets. The National ZMR dropped to slightly underperforming In order to add further context to sales, Zonda created the Zonda Market Ranking (ZMR). The ZMR accounts for both sales pace and volume, is seasonally adjusted, and is taken as a percentage relative to a baseline market average. Based on the percentage above or below baseline, markets are bucketed into performance groups ranging from significantly underperforming to significantly overperforming relative to historical activity. The map below shows a snapshot of top production markets by region. Zonda also offers the ZMR for entry-level, move-up/move-down, and high-end markets. Subscribers of the National Outlook report can access all top markets and the tiered breakdown in Zonda’s portal. Non-subscribers can access the tiered maps for the select 10 markets by clicking below. Zonda’s snapshot markets were split between 0% overperforming, 10% average, and 90% underperforming. Among Zonda’s top 55 major markets, 5% were overperforming , 25% were average , and 70% were underperforming . Importantly, the ZMR does not account for what it takes to sell a home. For example, securing a sale might still feel difficult in a significantly overperforming market, but if the incentives offered result in a sale, we count the sale. items.title: Mortgage Rates Climb Again, and Spring Could Still See Rates Above 7%
items.description: Mortgage Rates Climb Again, and Spring Could Still See Rates Above 7% Zillow expects mortgage rates to remain above 7% for the rest of 2026 through mid-2027, presenting a possible headwind for next year’s home shopping season. Written by Kara Ng on November 18, 2026 In short: Mortgage rates rose again after a hotter-than-expected October inflation report reinforced expectations for a December Fed hike. With new-lease rent growth picking up, shelter may offer the Fed less help in bringing inflation down in 2027. Mortgage rates turn higher after a hot October inflation report After a few weeks of easing from the recent peak, mortgage rates rose again. One contributor was the hot October Consumer Price Index (CPI) report, which cemented a December Fed rate increase and highlighted the possibility of a 50bp hike (roughly at 10% probability , as of November 18). Shelter was a major driver of October inflation, and Zillow expects housing inflation to keep firming . New-lease rents are growing at their fastest pace in 2025-2026, so they’re no longer pulling down housing inflation measures, and forecasts for on-market rents have been revised upward in recent months. In other words, while oil-related developments could ease some inflation pressure, firmer rent growth means the Fed may get less help from shelter in 2027. What’s the impact on housing? Pending sales fell sharply in October , as both the level of mortgage rates and the speed at which they rose led buyers to step back. Because pending sales are a leading indicator of closed sales, October’s drop means closed sales should be weaker this month. Zillow’s forecast for 2027 calls for mortgage rates to stay above 7% until around mid-year, with sales falling 3.5%. However, a slowdown elsewhere in the economy or faster progress on inflation would pull mortgage rates down sooner. With inventory forecast to rise about 11% next year, there should be enough supply to meet demand if buyers return. NYC Capital Markets: Volume Moderates but Remains on Track for Recovery Year After four quarters of sustained recovery, investment sales slowed in the third quarter. Dollar volume totaled $5.6 billion, a 30.7% quarter-over-quarter (QOQ) decline and the first quarter since Q2 2025 to fall short of at least $8.0 billion. Investor confidence, which had steadily improved over the last year, was tempered by rising interest rates, uncertainty around the broader economy and geopolitical conditions, and the historically consistent trend of an election cycle pause. Despite the slowdown, the year-to-date (YTD) dollar volume total of $22.0 billion remains virtually unchanged from the same period last year, while the year’s annualized pace of $29.3 billion would represent a 23.3% increase over the 2020 cyclical low. In Q3 2026, there were 517 transactions involving the sale of 578 properties—an 18.2% year-over-year (YOY) decrease in properties sold. Average pricing for core property types across New York City fell to $504 per square foot (psf), a 0.6% decrease from the 2025 average. Cap rates for core property types have continued to inch higher in 2026 and now stand at an average of 7.13%. Sector Highlights Office: Dollar volume in Q3 2026 dipped to $1.4 billion, bringing the YTD total to $5.5 billion, only 7.8% below the same period last year. Although activity remains muted compared to historical levels, the investor pool is steadily expanding, with deals this quarter completed by a diverse mix of institutional, REIT, private capital, and user-purchasers. The average deal size declined for the third consecutive quarter, to $46.8 million, as smaller private capital players deployed more capital into value-add strategies for discounted and underutilized assets. At the same time, larger investors remain attracted to well-positioned, sizeable Class A assets with favorable tenancy and capital improvement conditions. Pricing has declined nominally this year, down 4.2% to $478 psf. Multifamily: Although combined dollar volume for elevator and walk-up properties slowed to $1.1 billion in Q3 2026, the YTD total of $4.8 billion falls only 11.7% short of the total from the same period last year, which marked the strongest year since 2022. Similar to the office sector, multifamily demand is starkly bifurcated between market-rate, newly-constructed, often luxury assets versus majority-rent-regulated, deeply discounted offerings—though both segments are exhibiting encouraging momentum. Substantial renter demand has kept vacancy at historic lows and attracted a growing pool of capital from both core/core-plus investors as well as value-add players. Development: Volume pulled back slightly to $831.6 million in Q3 2026, but the sector remains on pace to finish at $5.0 billion: if achieved, 2026 and 2025 would be the only two years since 2019 to surpass that benchmark. Depressed land values and a still-limited supply pipeline continued to drive activity. That momentum, previously focused in Manhattan, has begun to spread to the city’s secondary markets: four out of the five largest development transactions this quarter were located in the Outer Boroughs, totaling $249.6 million across 1.3 million buildable square feet. Increased demand has continued to support pricing recovery, with the citywide price per buildable square foot rising 6.4% YOY to $227, the highest average since 2019. items.title: South Atlantic Apartment Supply Set to Rebound in 2027
items.description: South Atlantic Apartment Supply Set to Rebound in 2027 by Carl Whitaker Posted November 9, 2026 in Insights While supply pressure eases across much of the Sun Belt, the South Atlantic is heading the other way, with 2027 apartment deliveries forecast to climb above 2026 levels. After a pullback in 2026, new apartment supply across Delaware, DC, Maryland, North Carolina and Virginia is forecast to rise to over 41,900 units in 2027. That is an increase of more than 11,400 units, or roughly 38%, and a notable contrast with several Sun Belt peers, where lighter construction is translating into a thinner delivery pipeline. The increase is not evenly spread. Charlotte (up 5,186 units to 13,543) and Raleigh/Durham (up 4,186 to 9,441) account for more than 80% of the regional jump, while Richmond, Washington, DC and Greensboro also see more deliveries. Carolina markets enter 2027 with strong demand foundations, but more than one-third of Charlotte units are already offering concessions. The 2027 wave is also more concentrated in select submarkets than the metro-wide surge of 2023 and 2024, and total deliveries remain well below the 2024 peak of roughly 65,600 units. Even so, it will take a strong year of demand to absorb this much new supply. items.description: Pending Home Sales Decreased 4.7% in October, According to NAR Report Section Menu NAR Media Contacts Statistical Release Schedule Op-Eds & Letters to the Editor NAR Fact Sheet NAR in the News More November 18, 2026 Media Contact: Media Relations Residential Real Estate , Promoting Home Ownership , Financing & Credit , Mortgages & Home Financing Share Month-Over-Month 4.7% decrease in pending home sales Declines in all four regions Year-Over-Year 16.7% decrease in pending home sales Declines in all four regions WASHINGTON (November 18, 2026) – Pending home sales in October decreased by 4.7% month-over-month and 16.7% year-over-year, according to the National Association of REALTORS ® Pending Home Sales report . The report helps the real estate ecosystem—including agents, homebuyers and sellers—better understand the housing market by providing data on the level of home sales under contract. Month-over-month pending home sales declined in all four major U.S. regions. Year-over-year pending home sales also declined in all four regions. “October could mark the low point in contract signings for this housing cycle, as mortgage rates appear to have topped out,” said NAR Chief Economist Dr. Lawrence Yun. “Two consecutive months of record-low pending contracts point to very sluggish fourth-quarter home sales closings, and annual existing-home sales could be the lowest since the mid-1990s,” Yun added. “It is somewhat puzzling that home sales would fall to levels last seen three decades ago, even as the U.S. population has grown by roughly 75 million. Either sizable housing demand is building in the background, or the dream of homeownership is increasingly out of reach for many Americans.” October 2026 National Pending Home Sales 4.7% decrease month-over-month 16.7% decrease year-over-year October 2026 Regional Pending Home Sales Northeast 0.8% decrease month-over-month 11.1% decrease year-over-year Midwest 2.7% decrease month-over-month 14.0% decrease year-over-year South 6.3% decrease month-over-month 18.7% decrease year-over-year West 6.9% decrease month-over-month 20.3% decrease year-over-year At the local level, pending home sales fell year-over-year even in the strongest markets. Among the 50 largest metro areas, the following 10 markets posted the smallest annual declines in pending home sales, according to data from Realtor.com ® Economics: Cincinnati, OH-KY-IN (-4.7%) Austin-Round Rock-San Marcos, TX (-9.7%) Hartford-West Hartford-East Hartford, CT (-10.0%) Indianapolis-Carmel-Greenwood, IN (-11.3%) Chicago-Naperville-Elgin, IL-IN (-11.9%) Pittsburgh, PA (-12.4%) Nashville-Davidson-Murfreesboro-Franklin, TN (-12.7%) Buffalo-Cheektowaga, NY (-12.7%) Jacksonville, FL (-12.8%) Cleveland, OH (-12.8%) About the National Association of REALTORS ® The National Association of REALTORS ® is involved in all aspects of residential and commercial real estate. The term REALTOR ® is a registered collective membership mark that identifies a real estate professional who is a member of the National Association of REALTORS ® and subscribes to its strict Code of Ethics . For free consumer guides about navigating the homebuying and selling transaction processes—from written buyer agreements to negotiating compensation—visit facts.realtor . # # # The Pending Home Sales Index is a leading indicator for the housing sector, based on pending sales of existing homes. A sale is listed as pending when the contract has been signed but the transaction has not closed, though the sale usually is finalized within one or two months of signing. Pending contracts are good early indicators of upcoming sales closings. However, the amount of time between pending contracts and completed sales is not identical for all home sales. Variations in the length of the process from pending contract to closed sale can be caused by issues such as buyer difficulties with obtaining mortgage financing, home inspection problems, or appraisal issues. The index is based on a sample that covers about 40% of multiple listing service data each month. In developing the model for the index, it was demonstrated that the level of monthly sales-contract activity parallels the level of closed existing-home sales in the following two months. An index of 100 is equal to the average level of contract activity during 2001, which was the first year to be examined. By coincidence, the volume of existing-home sales in 2001 fell within the range of 5.0 to 5.5 million, which is considered normal for the current U.S. population. Vacancy fell across the Bay Area for the 12th consecutive quarter, to 3.9%, as new construction has not been able to keep up with increasing demand. Economy: Solid Fundamentals Bay Area nonfarm employment increased year-over-year (YOY) by 0.9% to over 4.0 million. At the same time, the unemployment rate declined by 40 basis points (bps) to 4.1%. Employment growth is expected to continue rising over the next 12 months. Median household income increased by 6.7% YOY, to $153,800, remaining the highest of all metropolitan markets in the US. While tech layoffs have persisted, the artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) sector continues to expand its hiring and concurrently leasing large blocks of space. Through the third quarter of 2026, Bay Area-based companies captured 75.9% ($324.5 billion) of venture capital funding into AI/ML in the U.S. Supply and Demand: Demand Outpaces Supply Vacancy fell across the Bay Area for the 12th consecutive quarter, to 3.9%, as new construction has not been able to keep up with increasing demand. Vacancy is down 110 bps YOY and currently sits at the lowest level since the fourth quarter of 2007. Net absorption has slowed in back-to-back quarters, as deliveries have been quiet, but remains positive, with 2,077 units absorbed in the third quarter. As the number of available units continues to dwindle, absorption may continue to slow until new supply meets demand. Units delivered in the third quarter totaled 969, up 306 units from the prior quarter but down by over 500 units YOY. Excluding the prior quarter, it was the lowest quarterly total since the second quarter of 2013. The pipeline, however, is growing, as units under construction have risen for five consecutive quarters, reaching 18,625 units through the third quarter. There are over 100,000 units proposed across the Bay Area, but development is not likely to see a significant uptick in the short term as rising construction costs and a difficult financing environment prove to be headwinds. However, strong market conditions and state housing mandates may help to counteract these challenges. San Francisco County is responsible for much of this growth, as it reached $3,756 per unit in the third quarter, an increase of over 15% YOY. San Francisco is showing no signs of slowing down having posted YOY rental growth greater than 10% for three consecutive quarters, a feat that has not occurred since 2001. items.title: Home Purchase Loans Fall to Lowest Third-Quarter Level Since 2012
items.description: Home Purchase Loans Fall to Lowest Third-Quarter Level Since 2012 by ATTOM Team | Nov 19, 2026 | Mortgage Origination , Real Estate News - Recent Articles Home purchase lending falls 9 percent quarter-over-quarter to 729,968 loans; Refinance lending drops 16 percent quarter-over-quarter to 561,290 loans IRVINE, Calif. – Nov. 19, 2026 — ATTOM , the leading provider of property data , AI-powered intelligence , and real estate analytics solutions, today released its U.S. Residential Property Mortgage Origination Report for the third quarter of 2026, showing purchase and refinance lending slowed from the previous quarter as mortgage rates climbed and home purchase loans fell to their lowest third-quarter level since 2012. A total of 1.29 million purchase and refinance mortgages secured by residential property (1 to 4 units) were originated in the third quarter, down 12 percent from the previous quarter and 15 percent from a year earlier. Total loan volume reached $498.1 billion, down 15 percent quarterly and 12 percent year-over-year. The quarterly slowdown was driven by declines in both home purchase and refinance lending. Purchase loans fell 9 percent from the previous quarter to 729,968, marking the lowest third-quarter total since 2012. Purchase loans were down 12 percent from a year earlier, even as the average purchase loan amount rose 3 percent over the same period to $411,756. “The increase in refinance activity we saw late last year and into early this year cooled in the third quarter, with refinancing declining more than purchase lending,” said Rob Barber, CEO of ATTOM. “Purchase loans also slipped to their lowest third-quarter level since 2012, as higher mortgage rates and elevated average purchase loan amounts continued to strain affordability for many buyers.” Purchase lending slips quarterly in most markets Purchase lending totaled $300.6 billion in the third quarter, down 10 percent from the previous quarter and 10 percent below year-ago levels. Purchase loans accounted for 56.5 percent of all purchase and refinance originations, up from 54.5 percent in both the second quarter of 2026 and the third quarter of 2025. Purchase activity declined quarterly in 73.6 percent of analyzed metro areas with a population of 200,000 or more and sufficient data. Among metros with populations above 1 million, the largest quarterly increases were in Buffalo, NY (up 61 percent); Memphis, TN (up 50 percent); Rochester, NY (up 32 percent); New York, NY (up 22 percent); and Hartford, CT (up 20 percent). The steepest quarterly drops among large metros were in Salt Lake City, UT; New Orleans, LA; Denver, CO; Atlanta, GA; and Richmond, VA. Refinancing activity falls sharply quarter-over-quarter Refinancing activity fell 16 percent quarter-over-quarter to 561,290 loans, the lowest quarterly total since the second quarter of 2024, and was 19 percent below the third quarter of 2025. Refinance originations accounted for 43.5 percent of all purchase and refinance loans, down from 45.5 percent in both the previous quarter and a year earlier. Refinance lending declined quarterly in 89.4 percent of analyzed metro areas, with the steepest quarterly drops among large metros in San Jose, CA; Dallas, TX; San Francisco, CA; Austin, TX; and Louisville, KY. FHA and VA loan shares decline quarterly Loans backed by the Federal Housing Administration accounted for 15.7 percent of all purchase and refinance originations in the third quarter, down from 16.1 percent in the second quarter and 17.9 percent a year earlier. VA-backed loans represented 6.9 percent of originations, down from 8.2 percent in the second quarter and 7.2 percent a year earlier, the lowest share since the second quarter of 2024. Mortgage rates climb above 7 percent by early October Mortgage rates trended higher during the quarter. According to Freddie Mac, the average rate on a 30-year fixed mortgage rose from 6.43 percent in early July to 7.28 percent by early October, adding pressure to an already constrained housing market. Home purchase lending dropped 9 percent quarter-over-quarter to 729,968 loans, the lowest third-quarter level since 2012, while refinance lending fell 16 percent quarter-over-quarter to 561,290 loans. Report methodology ATTOM analyzed recorded mortgage and deed of trust data for single-family homes, condos, town homes and multi-family properties of two to four units for this report. This report covers purchase and refinance loan originations. Each recorded mortgage or deed of trust was counted as a separate loan origination. Dollar volume was calculated by multiplying the total number of loan originations by the average loan amount for those loan originations. items.title: Annual rent growth sees a milestone, even as prices ease in October
items.description: Annual rent growth sees a milestone, even as prices ease in October by Kim O'Brien Posted November 6, 2026 in Market Research October marked the first month of rent cuts in the U.S. apartment market in 2026, but annual gains continue at a robust pace. Same-store effective asking rents increased 1.7% year-over-year, according to October data from RealPage Market Analytics . That was the market’s biggest annual price increase since May 2023. While the annual reading has improved, the gain stemmed less from robust monthly pricing and more from weak rent performance falling out of the annual calculation. In fact, rents came down a mild 0.7% during October, marking the first monthly rent cut in the U.S. in calendar 2026. U.S. apartment occupancy faded to 95% in October, easing 20 basis points (bps) from the September showing. Still, October occupancy is up 40 bps in the calendar year and remains 10 bps ahead of the October 2025 showing. Helping support occupancy and rent performance, the U.S. apartment market has seen supply and demand edge closer to balance recently. Renters absorbed nearly 304,800 conventional apartments in the year-ending 3rd quarter 2026, gaining ground on a cooling supply wave. Developers completed nearly 318,000 units in the past year, nearly half the recent peak from late 2024. Bay Area and Midwest markets still lead for rent growth Rent performance remained sharply split by market. Coastal tech hubs and Midwest metros delivered the strongest annual gains, while most Sun Belt markets kept logging rent declines. Northern California's tech-driven markets posted the three strongest gains among the 50 largest apartment markets in the year-ending October. San Francisco saw rents hike 14.7% over the past year, San Jose followed at 9.5%, and Oakland reached 8.5%. All three markets are running near 97% occupancy. Midwest markets make up much of the rest of the top 10 list. Milwaukee led the major Midwest markets with annual rent growth of 4.2%, followed by Chicago (3.3%), Kansas City (3.1%) and Cleveland (3.1%). Detroit and St. Louis both fell just shy of making the cut, with annual rent growth of 2.7% in each market. Sun Belt rents still trail, but the gap is narrowing The South region overall has returned to annual rent growth, though barely, at 0.5% in October. Sun Belt and Florida markets continue to see the nation’s steepest declines. San Antonio had the deepest cut among big markets at 2.6%, stemming from occupancy at 92.5%, also dead last among the largest 50 markets. Also posting rent declines in the year-ending October were Houston (-1.8%), Tampa (-1%), Charlotte (-0.9%) and Denver (-0.8%). The bigger story, however, is how many Sun Belt markets have stopped seeing rent positioning hemorrhage. Annual increases have returned to Phoenix (0.4%) and Austin (0.6%), as well as Atlanta (0.8%), Raleigh (1.0%), Miami (0.6%) and Jacksonville (2.6%). items.title: New Home Lot Supply Index
items.description: New Home Lot Supply Index The New Home Lot Supply Index provides an unrivaled look into the lot markets across the country, offering a current quarter snapshot as well as insight into the directional trend. This report details data for the third quarter of 2026. November 18, 2026 – 4 min read Table of Content: Zonda’s New Home Lot Supply Index (LSI) for 3Q26, rose for the ninth consecutive quarter and showed lot supply loosened both year-over-year and quarter-over-quarter across the United States. The index is a residential real estate indicator based on the number of single-family vacant developed lots (VDL) and the rate at which those lots are absorbed via housing starts. The New Home LSI came in at 88.5 for 3Q26, representing a 20.8% increase from 3Q25. This quarter, the market continued to be rated “appropriately supplied.” On a quarter-over-quarter basis, supply increased by 3.9% from 2Q26. The LSI counts the total vacant developed lot supply and adjusts it for overall starts activity. “The national lot market is moving more firmly into balance,” said Sean Fergus, vice president of economic research for Zonda. “But that balance needs to be viewed in the context of today’s housing market. Affordability pressures and widespread incentives underscore the challenges builders face in converting demand into sales. An appropriately supplied lot market means availability is better aligned with the current pace of construction; it does not mean the industry’s longer-term land constraints and cost challenges have disappeared.” In 2Q26, the LSI sat right on the boundary between "slightly undersupplied" and "appropriately supplied." However, the upward movement in Q3 solidified the national rating as “appropriately supplied.” In 3Q26, lot supply loosened year-over-year across all major metropolitan areas Zonda tracks, except Boise. For markets that saw an increase in lot supply, the average year-over-year gain was significant at +32%. More markets trended up and were rated “appropriately supplied” or “oversupplied” in the third quarter, but 12 out of 30 were still categorized as “significantly undersupplied.” The markets where land supply loosened the most on a year-over-year basis were Baltimore, Portland, and Seattle. Boise was the only market where local lot supply tightened compared to 3Q25, falling from 65.7 to 51.9, joining one of 12 markets rated “significantly undersupplied.” Eight markets changed ratings this quarter, as outlined in the chart below: Zonda also records future lots through the stages of development. The stages range from raw land through streets in, which is the last step before the lot becomes a vacant developed lot. Zonda groups the last few stages into a classification called total upcoming lots, which typically indicates delivery over the next 12-18 months. Total upcoming lots in 3Q26 increased 1.0% year-over-year and 1.6% quarter-over-quarter. These types of lots in the third quarter were down 12.2% from the 2022 peak but were up 23.4% compared to the same quarter in 2019. Among total upcoming lots, roadwork was down 15.3% year-over-year. Roadwork is comprised of the two smaller stages—streets paved and streets in—and represents the last step in lot development. Lots in the excavation stage were up 8.6% year-over-year, and those with equipment on site were up 5.7%. The largest share of total upcoming lots were in the excavation stage in 3Q26, totaling 416K. These lots have an expected delivery between 2Q27 and 3Q27 (the range represents different timeframes from local entitlement processes). Note, not all of the lots in excavation will match Zonda’s estimated timeline. “The development pipeline is edging higher, but the mix of activity matters,” Fergus said. “More lots are in excavation and equipment-on-site stages than a year ago, while fewer are in the final roadwork stages. That points to continued investment in future communities, but an uneven flow of near-term deliveries. items.title: October 2026 Rental Report: Rents Rise Annually for the First Time Since June 2023
items.description: October 2026 Rental Report: Rents Rise Annually for the First Time Since June 2023 By Jiayi Xu , Danielle Hale Nov 18, 2026 Highlights October 2026 marks the first month of year-over-year rent growth since June 2023. The change was modest with the median asking rent rising by just $1 (+0.1%) from October 2025 to $1,692. Rents continue to split the difference between their recent highs and prepandemic level. They are down $82 (-4.6%) from summer 2022 peak, and up $221 (+15%) from pre-pandemic level. Rent rebounded in larger units, while studio rents continue to soften: Studio: $1,411, down $17 (-1.2%) YoY 1-bed: $1,566, up $1(+0.1%) YoY 2-bed: $1,889, up $5 (+0.3%) YoY In 2026Q3, multifamily deliveries have returned to pre-pandemic levels as the 2021–2022 boom cohorts clear. Looking ahead, a cooling in starts suggests that new rental supply is likely to stay modest in the near term. Completions: 330,000, down 26% YoY Under Construction: 674,000, down 2.7% YoY Starts: 403,000, down 9.2% YoY All U.S. regions share the national pattern of cooling completions but differ in what comes next based on starts and the under-construction pipeline: the Northeast is rebuilding, the Midwest and South are easing from elevated levels, and the West looks the most likely to tighten. In October 2026, the median asking rent rose 0.1% year over year, the first annual increase since June 2023. Median asking rent for 0–2 bedroom properties across the 50 largest metro areas was $1,692, about $221 (15%) above the pre-pandemic level but $82 (-4.6%) below the August 2022 peak. Median asking rents fell year over year for more than three years, and the 2021–2022 multifamily construction boom was the main driver of the decline. Projects started in those years were delivered in 2023–2025 and added supply that held rents down. According to the Housing Vacancy Survey, the rental vacancy rate reached 7.6% in 2026Q3, the highest level since early 2014. However, as construction activity unwinds, the downward pressure on rents from new supply has eased. At the same time, elevated borrowing costs may be supporting rental demand by keeping more households renting. The path ahead largely depends on whether new multifamily deliveries remain strong enough to outpace that demand. Larger units see rents increase In October 2026, the median asking rent for two-bedroom units rose 0.3% year over year, the first annual increase since May 2023. At $1,889, the national median for two-bedroom units is $82 (4.2%) below its July 2022 peak. Even after more than three years of softness, it remains $299 (18.8%) above its level seven years ago. The rent for one-bedroom units increased 0.1% in October 2026 on a year over year basis, and now stands at $1,566. This was the first month of annual rent growth since June 2023. Rent was $95 (-5.7%) lower than the peak observed during August 2022, but still $191 (13.9%) higher than in October 2019. In October 2026, the median asking rent for studios fell by 1.2%, marking the 39th consecutive month of annual declines. The median rent of studios was $1,411 in October, down by $73 (-4.9%) from its peak, seen in Fall 2022. Nevertheless, the median asking rent for studios was still $141 (11.1%) higher than seven years ago. During this period, the newly completed units boosted the total rental stock by 3.2%, or a rate of more than 1% per year. This surge in deliveries was largely driven by the multifamily starts boom of 2021–2023, when 1,452,000 units were started (an average of 484,000 per year), 33% more than in 2017–2019. Because projects typically take about 1.5 years to complete , those starts translated into the wave of completions in 2023–2025. However, with the unwinding of the construction boom, in this October monthly report, we revisit the supply side of the equation to understand how the fade of that boom is shaping the outlook for construction pipelines as well as rents. items.title: New Residential Construction Press Release
items.description: FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE: Wednesday, November 18, 2026 MONTHLY NEW RESIDENTIAL CONSTRUCTION, OCTOBER 2026 November 18, 2026 CB26-187 Building Permits Privately-owned housing units authorized by building permits in October were at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1,295,000. This is 7.4 percent below the revised September rate of 1,398,000 and is 8.7 percent below the October 2025 rate of 1,418,000. Single-family authorizations in October were at a rate of 772,000; this is 8.7 percent below the revised September figure of 846,000. Authorizations of units in buildings with five units or more were at a rate of 475,000 in October. Housing Starts Privately-owned housing starts in October were at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1,309,000. This is 9.9 percent (±16.8 percent)* above the revised September estimate of 1,191,000 and is 2.8 percent (±16.5 percent)* above the October 2025 rate of 1,273,000. Single-family housing starts in October were at a rate of 864,000; this is 4.0 percent (±9.0 percent)* above the revised September figure of 831,000. The October rate for units in buildings with five units or more was 433,000. Housing Completions Privately-owned housing completions in October were at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1,272,000. This is 6.5 percent (±13.2 percent)* above the revised September estimate of 1,194,000, but is 10.4 percent (±11.6 percent)* below the October 2025 rate of 1,419,000. Single-family housing completions in October were at a rate of 900,000; this is 6.3 percent (±13.3 percent)* above the revised September rate of 847,000. The October rate for units in buildings with five units or more was 362,000. items.title: Mortgage Rates
items.description: Mortgage Rates Primary Mortgage Market Survey ® (PMMS ® ) results are based on the mortgage rate collected from thousands of loan applications submitted to Freddie Mac through Loan Product Advisor ® (LPA ® ) from lenders across the country when a borrower applies for a mortgage. Learn more in our FAQs. Primary Mortgage Market Survey ® U.S. weekly mortgage rate averages as of 11/19/2026 30-year Fixed-Rate Mortgage 7.28% 15-year Fixed-Rate Mortgage 6.66% Download Rates Since 1971 Mortgage Rates Average 7.28% While prospective borrowers often shop around for a home, they may not always think to do the same for their mortgage, as comparing multiple rate quotes can potentially save them thousands over a loan’s lifetime. The 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 7.28% as of November 19, 2026, up from last week when it averaged 7.11%. A year ago at this time, the 30-year FRM averaged 6.26%. The 15-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 6.66%, up from last week when it averaged 6.45%. A year ago at this time, the 15-year FRM averaged 5.54%. PMMS results are released weekly on Thursdays at 12 p.m. ET. and are an average of loan rates offered the prior Thursday through Wednesday. See our publication calendar . Compare Historical PMMS Results Frequently Asked Questions Toggle all accordion sections Expand All What data is used for PMMS? The PMMS results are based on data from our Loan Product Advisor (LPA): mortgage rates collected from thousands of loan applications submitted to Freddie Mac from lenders across the country when a borrower applies for a mortgage. For more detailed information, see Enhanced Mortgage Rate Survey Explained . How is the national average determined? We collect the mortgage rate of all purchase applications based on PMMS criteria and a national average mortgage rate is calculated out of all the selected loan applications. The criteria include weekly conventional, single-family originations with conforming loan limits as set by FHFA. Is the PMMS rate based on current lender quotes or recent settlements? PMMS rates are based on applications submitted to Freddie Mac for the given week from lenders across the country. What type of lenders are included in the PMMS? Currently, our lenders are a mix of credit unions, commercial banks and mortgage lending companies. Do the PMMS results represent the rates charged on a specific day of the week? If so, which day? Or are they the average rate charged that week? PMMS is published each Thursday at noon ET. When a U.S. holiday falls on a Thursday, the PMMS will publish on the Wednesday of that week. The week of application activity starts at 12:00 a.m. ET the prior Thursday and lasts through 11:59 p.m. ET Wednesday. Therefore, the PMMS results are an average of loan rates offered Thursday through Wednesday. See our publication calendar . Why are adjustable rates no longer published? ARMs indexed to alternatives to U.S. Treasury securities have become more prevalent in the market. As we worked on enhancing the PMMS , we carefully considered which loan products were most popular for the PMMS borrower profile (good/excellent credit, 20% loans, home purchase loans on owner occupied 1-unit single-family properties). Additionally, in recent years the mortgage market has been dominated by fixed mortgage products. While there has been an uptick recently in the share of adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs) for the broader mortgage market, ARMs remain most popular for higher loan size (nonconforming) loans. Why are fees/points no longer published? Under the current LPA requirements, fees and points are not always required to be provided by lenders. Therefore, we are not able to report on the average fees and points. How has PMMS changed over time? Since April 1971, Freddie Mac shared the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate with the PMMS. We have updated the information we collect and the process for gathering data over time. Changes in Data Processes When it was launched, PMMS surveyed lenders on the rates and points for their most popular 30-year fixed-rate, 15-year fixed-rate and 5/1 hybrid amortizing adjustable-rate mortgage products. The survey was based on first-lien prime conventional conforming home purchase mortgages with a loan-to-value of 80 percent. In addition, the adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) products were indexed to U.S. Treasury yields, and lenders were asked for both the initial coupon rate and points as well as the margin on the ARM products. Lenders surveyed each week were a mix of lender types — credit unions, commercial banks and mortgage lending companies — roughly proportional to the level of mortgage business that each type commands nationwide. On November 17, 2022, the mortgage rate gathering process was updated. Instead of surveying lenders, we now use data from our Loan Product Advisor (LPA). Changes in Information Shared In 1984 , the 1-year ARM was added to the survey. In 1991 , the 15-year fixed-rate mortgage rate was added. In January 2005 , a 5/1 hybrid ARM series was added. In January 2016 , the 1-year ARM was discontinued. In November 2022 , adjustable rates and fees/points were discontinued. For more detailed information, see Enhanced Mortgage Rate Survey Explained . executive_summary.text: 美国 10 月住宅签约量同比下降 16.7%，截至 11 月 19 日的 30 年期固定房贷利率升至 7.28%；Zillow 预计房贷利率将维持在 7% 以上至 2027 年年中前后，购房需求仍面临融资压力。高力指出，美国多户住宅开发管线继续收缩，租金回升范围扩大；但 RealPage 预计南大西洋地区 2027 年公寓交付反弹，当地能否吸纳新增供给值得关注。美国财政部拟限制 BTR 运营商收购获入住许可逾 18 个月的住宅，运营商担忧新开发受阻，仍需关注最终条款。
executive_summary.text_en: U.S. home contract signings fell 16.7% year over year in October, and the 30-year fixed mortgage rate rose to 7.28% as of November 19; Zillow expects mortgage rates to stay above 7% until around mid-2027, keeping financing pressure on buyer demand. Colliers finds that the U.S. multifamily development pipeline continues to shrink and rent recovery has broadened, but RealPage forecasts a rebound in South Atlantic apartment deliveries in 2027, making local absorption worth watching. The U.S. Treasury proposes barring BTR operators from buying homes more than 18 months after they receive a certificate of occupancy; operators warn that the rule could hinder new development, and the final terms bear watching.
